newsitem.title: USA: US Treasury official expects bank-insurance reform.
newsitem.headline: US Treasury official expects bank-insurance reform.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury undersecretary for domestic finance said Monday he expected Congress in its next session to pass a bill that will allow banks to sell insurance in some form.

"The prospects for real financial modernization coming about in the next Congress are extremely promising," the Treasury official, John Hawke, said in a speech to the Financial Institutions Insurance Association, a trade group.
"Financial modernization," he said, have become buzz words for allowing banks to market insurance.

Hawke said, however, that he sees one stumbling block. Insurance companies again will argue that banks have an unfair advantage because their deposits are federally insured, thereby allowing them to raise funds cheaper than they can.
Banks could use these deposits to fund their insurance operations, many in the insurance industry assert.
Therefore, they want banks to be forced to separate the two operations by having holding companies own them as individual subsidiaries.
Ultimately, he said, the insurance subsidiary would benefit the overall company.

After his address, Hawke explained in a brief interview that there are many ways that holding companies could achieve this, including by having the insurance subsidiary pay its parent dividends. "It's a phoney issue," Hawke said.
Asked then how could the playing field be leveled for insurance companies, he answered, "Let them buy banks."
In the interview he said he expected the legislation that Congress may adopt would either allow banks to sell insurance directly or to do so by affiliating with insurance carriers.
